title: Check your understanding: Git Remote Protocols

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of git remote protocols?
options: Git can exchange repository data over HTTPS, SSH and supported local/file transports. Authentication, host verification and protocol support depend on the server and environment, so avoid putting credentials directly in URLs.
Git automatically backs up every file, including ignored and untracked files, to a remote.
The operation grants every contributor write access to the hosted repository.
questions.answer_key: Git can exchange repository data over HTTPS, SSH and supported local/file transports. Authentication, host verification and protocol support depend on the server and environment, so avoid putting credentials directly in URLs.
questions.explanation: Git can exchange repository data over HTTPS, SSH and supported local/file transports. Authentication, host verification and protocol support depend on the server and environment, so avoid putting credentials directly in URLs.

questions.prompt: Which command is the most direct starting point for this lesson’s example?
questions.explanation: Use `git remote -v` as the first inspection/action in the example, and then verify the result with the companion checks in the lesson.

questions.prompt: Which is the safest general practice when working with git remote protocols?
options: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
Run the most destructive option first; the reflog guarantees every file can always be recovered.
Assume the local command also changed the remote and satisfied all hosting-platform policies.
questions.answer_key: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
questions.explanation: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
